system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2175-10-19 18:36:00 to 2175-10-20 13:37:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder, COPD, chronic pain, and hypertension, was admitted after presenting to the ED with alcohol intoxication, hypoxia, and cough. He was agitated and disoriented on arrival, with a high blood alcohol level and signs of possible early withdrawal. He received diazepam for withdrawal symptoms, along with oral thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. Despite medical recommendations to continue treatment for a suspected COPD exacerbation and incomplete pneumonia therapy, James refused further interventions, including nebulizers, physical exams, and ECG. He remained alert and oriented, with stable vitals, and chose to leave against medical advice. He was discharged home with instructions to resume his medications, stop drinking, and follow up with his primary care provider for ongoing management of COPD, hypertension, pain, and abnormal blood findings.
problems: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, continuous
Surgical or other procedure not carried out because of patient's decision
Other nonspecific findings on examination of blood

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. James, I’m Dr. Patel. You were brought in after being found slumped over. You’re at the hospital now. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay… just tired. What time is it? I need to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s early evening. We’re concerned because your blood pressure was low when you arrived, and you were very drowsy. You’ve had some fluids, and your pressure has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I drink sometimes. But I’m fine now. I don’t need to stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’ve had a lot of alcohol recently—your level was high. You also have COPD, and your oxygen was low. You needed 4 liters of oxygen at one point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I have breathing problems. But I’ve been through this before. I’ll rest when I get back out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows changes from emphysema and some collapse in the lower parts of your lungs—atelectasis. It’s not new, but it does make it harder to breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it pneumonia again? Last time they gave me antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did get one dose of levofloxacin in the ER. But you’re not running a fever, and your white count is normal, so we don’t think it’s active pneumonia. The atelectasis is likely from not coughing deeply, maybe due to pain or fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve got pain from old injuries. Car wreck years ago. But I can manage it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know you’ve had multiple fractures and a splenectomy. But right now, the main issues are the alcohol, your low blood pressure from dehydration, and your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to go. I’ve been in the hospital too many times. I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you were agitated earlier and needed sedation with Haldol. You were also in restraints for safety. That means you weren’t fully in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was confused, yeah. But I’m清醒 now. I know what I’m saying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were going to start a detox protocol and monitor you for withdrawal—given your history of seizures and DTs. Social work was also trying to file a Section 35 to help with involuntary hold, but the courts are closed today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want that. I’m not staying. I understand the risks—you told me last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I have to document that you’re leaving against medical advice. You’re alert now, and you say you understand—low blood pressure, breathing issues, risk of withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’m leaving. I’ll try to cut back on the drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You’re able to walk and are not short of breath right now. But please consider going to a shelter or clinic tomorrow to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks for the oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: James, I’m told you’re preparing to leave. Just confirming—you’re still making this choice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m leaving. I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve documented your condition as stable but leaving against medical advice. Please seek help if you start shaking, hallucinating, or can’t breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: James, you left the unit last night. We tried to reach you, but you were already gone. I’m glad you made it out safely, but I wish you’d stayed for detox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I walked out because I didn’t want to be held. I’m not sick enough to stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals were stable when you left, and you were alert. But your history puts you at high risk. Please follow up with someone—your primary care or a clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks for the care.

summary.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder, COPD, chronic pain from prior trauma, and hypertension, was admitted after being found unresponsive and intoxicated. He presented with hypotension and hypoxia, which improved with IV fluids and oxygen support. His condition was complicated by a high blood alcohol level, somnolence, and prior noncompliance with treatment. A chest X-ray showed chronic emphysematous changes and bibasilar atelectasis without acute pneumonia. He received one dose of levofloxacin in the emergency department but did not complete a full course. Due to agitation, he required Haldol and brief physical restraints. Despite plans to initiate detox and pursue a Section 35 hold, James insisted on leaving against medical advice. He was alert and ambulatory at discharge, with understanding of the risks, and was advised to seek follow-up care.
